name: Chisel
text: I’ll pull the full repo and transcript to establish a complete source baseline. First, I’ll clone the repo locally (`git clone <repo-url> .`) and verify the commit hash matches the transcript’s reference. Then I’ll run `wc -l *` across all files to count lines of code and text, flagging any binary or ignored files. Next, I’ll extract every unique symbol (functions, classes, variables) from the source using `ctags -R` and cross-reference them against the transcript’s named entities with `grep -oE '\b[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*\b' transcript.txt | sort -u`. This gives me the raw material to deep-analyze each element from its full context.

name: Sift
text: Sift here—your proposal stops at *counting lines* without explaining *why* that metric matters for the analysis goal. A line count is trivial unless you tie it to a hypothesis (e.g., "high line counts correlate with X risk"). What’s the *real* weakness you’re guarding against? Cite the transcript’s explicit risk criteria or repo patterns that justify this step—don’t just default to `wc -l` because it’s easy. Evidence or shut up.
